topic: What is a systematic investment plan (SIP) and how does it work
outline: How a SIP works step by step
Rupee cost averaging: what it does and does not do
Costs, lock-ins and rules to check
What happens if an instalment fails
facts: A SIP is a method of investing a fixed amount in a mutual fund scheme at regular intervals, such as monthly. It is not a separate product.
The investor chooses the scheme, the amount, the date and the frequency, and sets up an auto-debit instruction (mandate) with their bank.
On each date the amount buys units at that day's net asset value (NAV), so more units are allotted when the NAV is low and fewer when it is high.
This averaging of purchase cost is called rupee cost averaging. It reduces dependence on picking a single entry point but does not protect against losses or guarantee returns.
Mutual fund returns are not guaranteed and the NAV can fall as well as rise.
Minimum SIP amounts and available frequencies differ by fund house and scheme, so check the scheme documents.
Most open-ended funds have no lock-in, but ELSS tax-saving funds carry a 3-year lock-in that applies separately to each SIP instalment.
Some schemes charge an exit load if units are redeemed within a period set by the scheme, so check the scheme documents.
Gains are taxed under the rules in force at the time of redemption, and these rules change, so check the current rules.
KYC verification is required before investing in mutual funds.
Investors can usually pause or stop a SIP, subject to the fund house's rules and notice periods.
The right scheme depends on the investor's time horizon and risk tolerance.
A lump sum investment buys units at a single NAV on one date, while a SIP spreads purchases across several dates.
If a SIP instalment cannot be debited because the bank account has insufficient balance, that instalment is not invested, and the bank may charge a fee for the failed debit.
Fund houses may cancel a SIP after repeated failed debits, according to their own rules.
If a SIP date falls on a holiday, the instalment is typically processed on the next business day.
Direct plans and regular plans of the same scheme differ in expenses, because regular plans include a distributor commission.
Mutual funds in India are regulated by SEBI, and AMFI publishes NAVs and investor information.
The scheme information document and the fact sheet list the investment objective, expenses, exit load and risk level of a scheme.
title: What Is a SIP and How Does It Work?

topic: Term insurance versus endowment plans: the basic difference
outline: Premiums and what they depend on
facts: A pure term plan pays the sum assured to the nominee if the policyholder dies during the policy term; it pays nothing if the policyholder survives the term.
An endowment plan combines life cover with savings: it pays a death benefit during the term and a maturity benefit if the policyholder survives.
Because part of an endowment premium goes to the savings component, premiums are generally higher than for a pure term plan with the same life cover.
Some term plans offer a return of premium option, which raises the premium.
In traditional endowment plans, only part of the maturity amount may be guaranteed; bonuses, where offered, are not guaranteed.
Compare the sum assured, policy term, premium payment term, exclusions, and the insurer's claim settlement record.
Exclusions and conditions differ by insurer and are listed in the policy document.
Health and lifestyle details must be disclosed accurately at purchase, since non-disclosure can lead to a claim being rejected.
Insurers in India are regulated by the IRDAI.
Insurance needs differ by person; this article is educational and not a recommendation of any plan.
This article compares two kinds of life insurance plan: term plans and endowment plans.
A term plan premium depends on factors such as the policyholder age, the sum assured, the policy term and the insurer assessment of health and lifestyle.
The policy term and the premium payment term can differ in some plans, so check both in the policy document.
Surrendering an endowment plan before maturity can return less than the premiums paid, depending on the surrender terms in the policy.
The claim settlement ratio is a published figure showing the share of claims an insurer settled in a year, and it does not predict how any individual claim will be treated.
The policyholder names a nominee to receive the benefit, and nominee details can be updated as circumstances change.
Riders such as accidental death or critical illness cover can be added to some plans for an additional premium, and the available riders differ by insurer and plan.
Tax treatment of premiums and benefits depends on the rules in force at the time, which change, so check the current rules.
A free-look period lets a policyholder review a new policy and return it if the terms are not acceptable, subject to the insurer rules.
title: Term Insurance vs Endowment Plans: Key Differences
